Unbelieving
un-bē-lēv'-ing
adj. (not believing; without faith; of a spouse, a Jew, a defiled conscience, and the damned)
From un- and believing. The New Testament word is apistos — literally faithless — and it functions as a settled category rather than a description of a mood: a man is either in the faith or he is not.

Biblical Definition

Paul's hardest pastoral case uses this word twice in two verses. To believers married to unconverted spouses: “the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy” (1Co 7:14). The sanctification here is not salvation — Paul asks two verses later how the believing spouse knows whether the other will be saved — but a covenantal setting-apart: the household stands under the gospel's influence rather than being defiled by the unbeliever's presence, and the children have a place in it. Hence the rule: do not leave. And the corresponding rule if the unbeliever leaves: “if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace” (1Co 7:15). Titus gives the moral effect of unbelief: “Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled” (Tit 1:15) — the problem is not the object but the eye. And Revelation puts the word in the most sobering list in Scripture: “the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers… shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone” (Rev 21:8). Unbelief stands second, before murder.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unbelieving as not believing, withholding belief, or infidel — and specifically, not believing the divine revelation.

expand to see more

UNBELIEVING, a. Not believing; withholding belief, particularly in divine revelation.

1. Infidel; not believing the truths of the gospel.

UNBELIEF, n. Incredulity; the withholding of belief; particularly, disbelief of divine revelation, or the doctrines of Christianity.

INFIDEL, n. One who disbelieves and rejects Christianity.

Key Scripture

1Co 7:14 — "For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy."

1Co 7:15 — "But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace."

Rev 21:8 — "But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death."

Tit 1:15 — "Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled."

Modern Corruption

Unbelief is treated as a neutral intellectual position; Revelation lists it among the sins that end in the second death.

expand to see more

The modern mind classes unbelief as a lack — the absence of a conviction, morally weightless, a matter of evidence and temperament. Scripture classes it as a sin, and Revelation 21:8 sets it second in a list that runs on to murderers and idolaters. The reason is that unbelief is not primarily an intellectual verdict but a refusal of testimony: he that believeth not God hath made him a liar (1Jo 5:10). John 3 says the condemnation is that light is come into the world and men loved darkness rather than light. That is a moral account of unbelief, and it is the Bible's.

The pastoral half of the word must be handled with equal care, because 1 Corinthians 7 is constantly misused in both directions. It does not teach that a believing spouse saves the other — Paul explicitly leaves that open. And it does not license a believer to leave an unconverted husband or wife: let him not put her away. What it grants is peace when the unbeliever departs, and hope while he stays. Peter adds the method for the wife in that house: without the word, won by the conversation of the wives (1Pe 3:1-2). Long obedience, not argument, is the instrument God most often uses there.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apistos (G571), without faith, unbelieving, faithless; apeitheo (G544), to refuse to be persuaded; hagiazo (G37), to set apart, sanctify.

expand to see more

Greek apistos (G571) — unbelieving, faithless, an unbeliever; 1 Corinthians 7:14-15, Titus 1:15, Revelation 21:8.

Greek hagiazo (G37) — to set apart, to sanctify; 1 Corinthians 7:14, of the unbelieving spouse set apart by the believing one.

Greek douloo (G1402) — to enslave, to bring into bondage; 1 Corinthians 7:15, the believer is not under bondage.

Greek apeitheo (G544) — to be disobedient, to refuse belief; John 3:36, he that believeth not the Son shall not see life.

Greek deuteros thanatos (G1208, G2288) — the second death; Revelation 20:14, 21:8.

Usage

"“The unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife” — set apart, not saved."

"“If the unbelieving depart, let him depart” — and God hath called us to peace."

"“The fearful, and unbelieving” — second in the list, before murderers."
